newsitem.title: USA: NYC agency urges accepting Brooklyn hospital lease.
newsitem.headline: NYC agency urges accepting Brooklyn hospital lease.

text.p: Two committees of New York City's Health and Hospitals Corp on Friday recommended that its board approve a plan to sublet Coney Island Hospital to a for-profit company, PHS NY, an agency spokesman said.
When there will be a full vote by the board has yet to be determined, but Maria Mitchell, the chairwoman of the Health and Hospitals Corp, told reporters, "That will occur rather quickly."
The agreement calls for the company to sublet the hospital, which is located in Brooklyn, for 99 years. When the deal closes, PHS NY will pay $42.1 million to the city's Health and Hospitals Corp.
The company, an affiliate of PHS Inc, which runs health-care companies in Cleveland and Philadelphia, also will pay $6.9 million to amortize debt linked to the hospital after the initial payment.
New York City, which owns 11 hospitals, is trying to lease or sell three of them as part of its new strategy of shifting functions to the private sector to cut costs.

The preliminary sublease agreement in mid-August was criticized sharply by City Comptroller Alan Hevesi, who questioned whether it would in fact save the city the $100 million that was estimated. And two board members have sued over the way in which the agreement was reached, but the city has yet to file its response, a spokesman for the Health and Hospitals Corp said.

And spokesman for Hevesi said he has urged the Health and Hospitals Corp to seek an opinion from the federal Internal Revenue Service on whether the proposed lease would jeopardize the tax-exempt status of bonds issued for the hospital.

The bond counsel for the city agency, Hawkins, Delafield & Wood, in a letter to the agency board, on Thursday said that the bonds would not become taxable if "safe-harbor" tax provisions and a process, called remediation, were used.

The bond counsel's letter, which the board discussed on Thursday, along with several other issues, like how PHS NY would safeguard the care of indigent patients, said that the hospital has up to $17 million of bonds outstanding.

Further, New York City has as much as $34 million of debt outstanding for Coney Island Hospital, the bond counsel wrote, though it noted its analysis only addressed the hospital's bonds. New York City has a separate law firm for its own debt.
Karen Shaw, a senior vice president on Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's staff, said that the city was confident that the tax-exempt status of the outstanding issues would be protected.

"We will be nothing nothing to undermine the tax-exempt status," she said. Shaw added she expected the analysis provided by the city's bond counsel to follow the sames lines as that done by Hawkins, Delafield & Wood.

The strategy the agency's counsel recommended to preserve the tax-exempt status of the hospital's bonds includes having it use $16 million of the money it gets from PHS-NY or the agency's equity for capital expenditures within 12 months after the hospital is subleased.
The privatization official did not dislcose how the money would be spent to take advantage of the remediation loophole.
